widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def beta_and_s2(cols, y):
    y = np.array(y, dtype=float)
    n, k = len(y), len(cols)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n)] + list(cols))
    beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
    resid = y - X @ beta
    s2 = (resid @ resid) / (n - k - 1)
    return list(beta) + [s2]

screens.title: Why $F = t^2$
screens.prose: Prove it for one predictor, with $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar x)^2$. Put the steps in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\hat y_i - \bar y = \hat\beta_1(x_i - \bar x)$, since the line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$; so $\mathrm{SSR} = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx}$
$= \dfrac{\mathrm{SSR}/1}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)} = F$, using line 1 on top and $s^2 = \mathrm{SSE}/(n - 2)$ below

hints.text: The first two lines are ingredients; either can come first.
Square $t$ only once you have both ingredients.
SSR and SE first, then $t^2$, then recognise $F$.

byKey.f: Recognising $F$ is the last step: it needs $t^2$ written out first.

explain.text: With one predictor, $t^2 = \hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx}/s^2$ and $F = \mathrm{SSR}/s^2$ are the same number. The $p$-values agree because an $F(1, \nu)$ variable is the square of a $t_\nu$ variable.

screens.title: The whole recipe
screens.prose: Every number in the summary comes from $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, the residuals and two degrees of freedom: $$\begin{aligned} s^2 &= \tfrac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n - k - 1}, & \mathrm{SE}_j &= \sqrt{s^2[(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}}, \\ t_j &= \hat\beta_j/\mathrm{SE}_j, & p_j &= 2P(T_{n-k-1} > |t_j|), \\ R^2 &= 1 - \tfrac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}, & F &= \tfrac{\mathrm{SSR}/k}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n - k - 1)}. \end{aligned}$$

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

def ols_summary(cols, y):
    y = np.array(y, dtype=float)
    n, k = len(y), len(cols)
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n)] + list(cols))
    XtX_inv = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
    beta = XtX_inv @ X.T @ y
    resid = y - X @ beta
    sse = resid @ resid
    sst = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    df = n - k - 1
    s2 = sse / df
    bse = np.sqrt(s2 * np.diag(XtX_inv))
    t = beta / bse
    p = 2 * stats.t.sf(np.abs(t), df)
    r2 = 1 - sse / sst
    r2_adj = 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / df
    F = ((sst - sse) / k) / (sse / df)
    F_p = stats.f.sf(F, k, df)
    return {"params": beta, "scale": s2, "bse": bse,
            "tvalues": t, "pvalues": p, "rsquared": r2,
            "rsquared_adj": r2_adj, "fvalue": F,
            "f_pvalue": F_p}

ideas: $s^2 = \mathrm{SSE}/(n - k - 1)$: every fitted coefficient, the intercept included, costs one degree of freedom.
Standard errors are square roots of the diagonal of $s^2(\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X})^{-1}$; $t = \hat\beta/\mathrm{SE}$ and its $p$ comes from $t_{n-k-1}$, not the normal.
$F = \frac{\mathrm{SSR}/k}{\mathrm{SSE}/(n - k - 1)}$ tests all slopes at once; with one predictor $F = t^2$.
